dedupe_keys.name: new north zealand hospital hillerød siting and rainwater design of a new acute hospital against extreme rain and high groundwater denmark

description: This case describes how a large new acute hospital north of Copenhagen was sited and designed to cope with heavier rain and rising groundwater. It is published by Climate-ADAPT, the European Environment Agency's adaptation platform, from information supplied by the Capital Region of Denmark. The New North Zealand Hospital merges three hospitals, covers 118,000 square metres with over 570 single rooms and serves more than 310,000 people. The content covers the climate challenge (rainfall projected to rise 6 to 9 percent by 2040-2070 on a low, wet site), the analysis (borehole groundwater response to rain, ten years of rainfall records, downscaled projections and 100-year 24 and 48-hour rain events), and the solutions: setting the building at an optimum level, ponds and streams to store and move water away from access roads, car park trenches and vegetated storage, and a layout that lets offices or clinics be converted into patient rooms. It reports a cost of about DKK 5.4 billion, construction from 2019 to handover in 2025, and a 50-year design life for the measures. The case is free and available to read online, with no data files to download. Caveats: a narrative account without the underlying model results, and coverage is one hospital. Simulation uses: an example for setting design rainfall and groundwater levels for critical health facilities and for planning surge bed capacity. Related records: the Førde hospital flood protection (case_study-forde-hospital-flood-protection) and the Caribbean smart hospitals initiative (case_study-caribbean-smart-hospitals).

name: New North Zealand Hospital, Hillerød: siting and rainwater design of a new acute hospital against extreme rain and high groundwater, Denmark
outcomes: The hospital (118,000 m2, over 570 single rooms, serving more than 310,000 people, about DKK 5.4 billion) was placed at an optimum level from groundwater modelling, with ponds, streams, car park trenches and vegetated areas storing rainwater and a layout that allows rooms to be converted if more beds are needed; handover in 2025, measures planned to last 50 years.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study on the Capital Region of Denmark
resources_used: Downscaled climate projections (A1B, RCP4.5, RCP8.5) and 100-year 24 and 48-hour rain events
